# Subring Generated by the Unity of a Ring with Unity

## 0. Conventions, statement, and a correction

**Conventions.** Throughout, $(R,+,\circ)$ is a *ring with unity*: an associative ring whose
multiplication $\circ$ possesses an identity element $1_R$, and — following the convention used
in the source of the statement, where a ring with unity is a *non-null* ring whose monoid
$(R\setminus\{0_R\},\circ)$ has an identity — we assume
$$1_R \neq 0_R .$$
(Section 7 explains what happens under the opposite convention.)

For $n \in \Z$ and $x$ an element of an additively written abelian group $(A,+)$, the symbol
$n x$ denotes the $n$-th power of $x$ in additive notation, i.e. the integer multiple defined
recursively by
$$0 x = 0_A, \qquad (n+1) x = n x + x \quad (n \ge 0), \qquad n x = -\bigl((-n) x\bigr) \quad (n < 0).$$

A *ring homomorphism* $h : (A,+,\cdot) \to (B,+,\circ)$ is a map satisfying
$h(a+b) = h(a)+h(b)$ and $h(a \cdot b) = h(a) \circ h(b)$ for all $a,b \in A$; it is **not**
required to map unity to unity. An *epimorphism* is a surjective homomorphism, a
*monomorphism* an injective one, and an *isomorphism* a bijective one. A homomorphism is
*nonzero* if it is not the constant map $a \mapsto 0_B$.

An element $x \in R$ is a *proper zero divisor* if $x \neq 0_R$ and there exists $y \neq 0_R$
with $x \circ y = 0_R$ or $y \circ x = 0_R$. Hence "$R$ has no proper zero divisors" means
$$\forall x, y \in R : \quad x \circ y = 0_R \ \Longrightarrow\ x = 0_R \ \text{ or }\ y = 0_R.
\tag{NZD}$$

Notation: $(x)$ denotes the principal ideal generated by $x$ (this is the object written with
the principal-ideal brackets in the problem statement); in $\Z$ we have $(n) = n\Z$. The subring of $R$ generated by a subset
$X \subseteq R$ — the intersection of all subrings of $R$ containing $X$, equivalently the
smallest such subring — is written $\langle X \rangle$. Finally $\Z_n := \Z / n\Z$, whose
elements are the residue classes $[a]_n = a + n\Z$.

Throughout, $g : \Z \to R$ is the map $g(n) = n 1_R$, and $S := \langle 1_R \rangle$.

**A correction to the statement.** Read literally, the last paragraph of the problem (the
dichotomy for $\ker g$) is asserted for an *arbitrary* ring with unity, and in that generality
it is **false**. Take $R = \Z_4$, a ring with unity $1_R = [1]_4 \neq [0]_4$. Then
$g(n) = [n]_4$ and
$$\ker g = 4\Z = (4),$$
which is neither $(0)$ nor $(p)$ for a prime $p$; correspondingly $S = \Z_4$ is not isomorphic
to any field, since $[2]_4 \neq [0]_4$ satisfies $[2]_4 [2]_4 = [0]_4$ and so is not
invertible. The hypothesis "$R$ has no proper zero divisors", introduced in the immediately
preceding paragraph of the statement, must therefore be carried over to the dichotomy. Under
that hypothesis the dichotomy is true, and this is what is proved below (Theorem C); Theorem D
records what survives for a general ring with unity. Note also that, since $\ker g$ is an ideal
of $\Z$, the "principal ideal generated by $0_R$" of alternative $(1)$ is to be read as the
zero ideal
$(0) = \{0\}$ of $\Z$.

Precisely, we prove the following.

> **Theorem A.** $g : \Z \to R$, $g(n) = n 1_R$, is a ring homomorphism whose image is exactly
> $S = \langle 1_R\rangle$, the subring of $R$ generated by $1_R$. Hence $g$ is an epimorphism
> from the ring $(\Z,+,\times)$ onto $S$.
>
> **Theorem B.** If $R$ has no proper zero divisors, then $g$ is the only nonzero ring
> homomorphism from $\Z$ into $R$.
>
> **Theorem C.** If $R$ has no proper zero divisors, then either
> $(1)$ $\ker g = (0)$, in which case $g$ is an isomorphism from $\Z$ onto $S$; or
> $(2)$ $\ker g = (p)$ for some prime $p$, in which case $S$ is isomorphic to the field $\Z_p$.
>
> **Theorem D** (general case). For an arbitrary ring with unity $R$ we have $\ker g = (n)$
> for a unique integer $n \ge 0$; necessarily $n \neq 1$; and $S \cong \Z_n$, where
> $\Z_0 := \Z$. The dichotomy of Theorem C can genuinely fail without (NZD).

**Induction over $\Z$.** We repeatedly use the following principle. *Let $P(n)$ be a property
of integers such that $P(0)$ holds and such that, for every $n \in \Z$, $P(n)$ implies both
$P(n+1)$ and $P(n-1)$. Then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \Z$.* Indeed, ordinary induction on
$k \ge 0$ using the step $P(n) \Rightarrow P(n+1)$ shows that $P(k)$ holds for all $k \ge 0$,
and ordinary induction on $k \ge 0$ using the step $P(n) \Rightarrow P(n-1)$ shows that
$P(-k)$ holds for all $k \ge 0$; together these exhaust $\Z$.

## 1. Preliminaries on integer multiples

**Lemma 1.** Let $(A,+)$ be an abelian group, $a \in A$ and $m,n \in \Z$. Then:

1. $1a = a$; $(n+1) a = n a + a$ and $(n-1) a = n a - a$;
2. $(m+n) a = m a + n a$;
3. $(m n) a = m (n a)$;
4. $(-n) a = -(n a)$;
5. in the ring $\Z$ itself, $n \cdot 1 = n$ for all $n \in \Z$ (the integer multiple $n\cdot 1$
   of the element $1 \in \Z$ equals $n$).

*Proof.* (i) $1a = (0+1)a = 0a + a = 0_A + a = a$ by the defining recursion. We prove
$(n+1)a = na + a$ for all $n \in \Z$ by cases.

*Case $n \ge 0$:* this is the defining recursion.

*Case $n = -1$:* $(n+1)a = 0a = 0_A$, while $na + a = (-1)a + a = -(1a) + a = -a + a = 0_A$.

*Case $n \le -2$:* put $m = -n \ge 2$. Then $n + 1 < 0$ and $-(n+1) = m - 1 \ge 1$, so by
definition $(n+1) a = -\bigl((m-1) a\bigr)$. On the other hand $na = -(ma)$ by definition, and
$m a = (m-1) a + a$ by the recursion (legitimate since $m - 1 \ge 0$), so, using that $A$ is
abelian and $-(x+y) = -x - y$,
$$n a + a = -\bigl((m-1)a + a\bigr) + a = \bigl(-a - (m-1)a\bigr) + a = -\bigl((m-1) a\bigr).$$
Hence $(n+1)a = na + a$ in all cases. Replacing $n$ by $n-1$ in this identity gives
$na = (n-1)a + a$, i.e. $(n-1) a = n a - a$.

(ii) Fix $m \in \Z$ and let $P(n)$ be the statement $(m+n) a = m a + n a$. $P(0)$ holds because
$0a = 0_A$. Assume $P(n)$. Then, by (i) applied twice (once to $m+n$, once to $n$),
$$\bigl((m+n)+1\bigr) a = (m+n) a + a = (m a + n a) + a = m a + \bigl(n a + a\bigr) = m a + (n+1) a,$$
which is $P(n+1)$; and
$$\bigl((m+n)-1\bigr) a = (m+n) a - a = (m a + n a) - a = m a + (n a - a) = m a + (n-1) a,$$
which is $P(n-1)$. By induction over $\Z$, $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \Z$.

(iii) Fix $n \in \Z$ and let $Q(m)$ be the statement $(m n) a = m (n a)$. $Q(0)$ holds since
both sides are $0_A$. Assume $Q(m)$. Using (ii) and then (i),
$$\bigl((m+1) n\bigr) a = (m n + n) a = (m n) a + n a = m (n a) + n a = (m+1)(n a),$$
$$\bigl((m-1) n\bigr) a = (m n - n) a = (m n) a - n a = m (n a) - n a = (m-1)(n a),$$
where in the second line we used (ii) in the form $(mn - n)a = (mn)a + (-n)a$ together with
(iv) below, whose proof is independent of (iii). By induction over $\Z$, $Q(m)$ holds for all
$m \in \Z$.

(iv) For $n < 0$ this is the definition. For $n = 0$ both sides equal $0_A$. For $n > 0$ we have
$-n < 0$, so by definition $(-n) a = -\bigl((-(-n)) a\bigr) = -(n a)$.

(v) Let $P(n)$ be "$n \cdot 1 = n$". $P(0)$ holds as $0 \cdot 1 = 0$. If $n \cdot 1 = n$ then by
(i) $(n+1)\cdot 1 = n \cdot 1 + 1 = n+1$ and $(n-1) \cdot 1 = n \cdot 1 - 1 = n - 1$. Induction
over $\Z$ gives the claim. $\square$

**Corollary to Lemma 1(iii),(v).** In the ring $\Z$, the integer multiple "$m$ times the element
$n$" coincides with the ring product $m n$: indeed $m\, n = m (n \cdot 1) = (m n)\cdot 1 = mn$.
So no ambiguity arises from the notation $mn$ inside $\Z$.

**Lemma 2.** Let $\phi : (A,+) \to (B,+)$ be a homomorphism of abelian groups. Then
$\phi(n a) = n\, \phi(a)$ for all $n \in \Z$ and $a \in A$.

*Proof.* A group homomorphism satisfies $\phi(0_A) = 0_B$ and $\phi(-x) = -\phi(x)$. Let $P(n)$
be "$\phi(n a) = n \phi(a)$". $P(0)$: $\phi(0 a) = \phi(0_A) = 0_B = 0\,\phi(a)$. Assume $P(n)$;
then by Lemma 1(i),
$$\phi\bigl((n+1) a\bigr) = \phi(n a + a) = \phi(n a) + \phi(a) = n \phi(a) + \phi(a) = (n+1)\phi(a),$$
$$\phi\bigl((n-1) a\bigr) = \phi(n a - a) = \phi(n a) - \phi(a) = n \phi(a) - \phi(a) = (n-1)\phi(a).$$
Induction over $\Z$ completes the proof. $\square$

**Lemma 3.** Let $(R,+,\circ)$ be a ring, $x,y \in R$ and $m,n \in \Z$. Then
$$(m x) \circ (n y) = (m n)(x \circ y).$$
Moreover $x \circ (y - z) = x\circ y - x \circ z$ and $(y-z)\circ x = y \circ x - z\circ x$ for
all $x,y,z \in R$.

*Proof.* For fixed $x \in R$, the map $\lambda_x : R \to R$, $\lambda_x(r) = x \circ r$,
satisfies $\lambda_x(r+s) = x \circ (r+s) = x\circ r + x \circ s$ by left distributivity, so
$\lambda_x$ is an endomorphism of the abelian group $(R,+)$. Likewise, for fixed $z \in R$ the
map $\rho_z(r) = r \circ z$ is an endomorphism of $(R,+)$ by right distributivity. The two
"moreover" identities are the statement that these endomorphisms preserve differences.
By Lemma 2 applied to $\lambda_x$ we get $x \circ (n y) = n (x \circ y)$; by Lemma 2 applied to
$\rho_z$ we get $(m x) \circ z = m (x \circ z)$. Combining, with $z := n y$, and using
Lemma 1(iii),
$$(m x) \circ (n y) = m\bigl(x \circ (n y)\bigr) = m\bigl(n (x \circ y)\bigr) = (m n)(x \circ y). \qquad \square$$

## 2. Theorem A

**Theorem A.** The map $g : \Z \to R$, $g(n) = n 1_R$, is a ring homomorphism; its image
$g[\Z] = \{ n 1_R : n \in \Z\}$ is precisely the subring $S = \langle 1_R \rangle$ of $R$
generated by $1_R$; consequently $g$ is an epimorphism from the ring $(\Z,+,\times)$ onto $S$.

*Proof.* **(a) $g$ is a ring homomorphism.** For $m,n \in \Z$, Lemma 1(ii) gives
$$g(m+n) = (m+n) 1_R = m 1_R + n 1_R = g(m) + g(n),$$
and Lemma 3 together with $1_R \circ 1_R = 1_R$ gives
$$g(m) \circ g(n) = (m 1_R) \circ (n 1_R) = (m n)(1_R \circ 1_R) = (m n) 1_R = g(m n).$$

**(b) $g[\Z]$ is a subring of $R$ containing $1_R$.** It is nonempty, as $0_R = 0\cdot 1_R = g(0)$.
By Lemma 1(iv), $-g(n) = -(n 1_R) = (-n) 1_R = g(-n)$, so by (a)
$$g(m) - g(n) = g(m) + g(-n) = g\bigl(m + (-n)\bigr) = g(m-n) \in g[\Z],$$
and $g(m) \circ g(n) = g(mn) \in g[\Z]$. Thus $g[\Z]$ is a nonempty subset of $R$ closed under
subtraction and under $\circ$; hence it is a subgroup of $(R,+)$ closed under multiplication,
i.e. a subring of $R$ (associativity of $\circ$ and distributivity are inherited from $R$).
Finally, by Lemma 1(i), $1_R = 1\cdot 1_R = g(1) \in g[\Z]$.

**(c) $g[\Z]$ is contained in every subring containing $1_R$.** Let $T$ be a subring of $R$ with
$1_R \in T$. Then $T$ is a subgroup of $(R,+)$, so $0_R \in T$ and $T$ is closed under $+$ and
$-$. Let $P(n)$ be "$n 1_R \in T$". $P(0)$ holds since $0\cdot 1_R = 0_R \in T$; and if
$n 1_R \in T$ then, by Lemma 1(i), $(n+1)1_R = n 1_R + 1_R \in T$ and
$(n-1) 1_R = n 1_R - 1_R \in T$. By induction over $\Z$, $n 1_R \in T$ for every $n \in \Z$,
i.e. $g[\Z] \subseteq T$.

**(d) Conclusion.** Let $\mathcal T$ be the family of all subrings of $R$ containing $1_R$ and
$S = \bigcap_{T \in \mathcal T} T$ the subring generated by $1_R$. By (b), $g[\Z] \in \mathcal T$,
so $S \subseteq g[\Z]$; by (c), $g[\Z] \subseteq T$ for every $T \in \mathcal T$, so
$g[\Z] \subseteq S$. Hence $g[\Z] = S$. (In particular the intersection $S$ is indeed a
subring, being equal to $g[\Z]$, and it is the smallest subring of $R$ containing $1_R$.)

Since $g$ is a homomorphism with image $S$, its corestriction $g : \Z \to S$ is a surjective
ring homomorphism, i.e. an epimorphism from $\Z$ onto $S$. $\square$

**Remark on conventions.** Some authors require a subring to contain $1_R$. The proof above is
insensitive to this: in step (c) only closure of $T$ under $+$ and $-$ and the assumption
$1_R \in T$ were used, and in step (b) the subring $g[\Z]$ was shown to contain $1_R$. Hence
under either convention $g[\Z]$ is the smallest subring of $R$ containing $1_R$, and $S$ denotes
the same set.

**Remark.** $S$ is a *commutative* ring with unity $1_R$: for $u = g(m)$, $v = g(n)$ in $S$ we
have $u \circ v = g(mn) = g(nm) = v\circ u$, and $1_R = g(1) \in S$ is an identity for $\circ$
on $S$ because it is one on $R$.

## 3. Theorem B

**Theorem B.** Assume $R$ has no proper zero divisors, i.e. (NZD) holds. Then $g$ is the only
nonzero ring homomorphism from $\Z$ into $R$.

*Proof.* By Theorem A, $g$ is a ring homomorphism, and it is nonzero because
$g(1) = 1 \cdot 1_R = 1_R \neq 0_R$ (Lemma 1(i) and the convention $1_R \ne 0_R$).

Conversely, let $h : \Z \to R$ be any ring homomorphism and set $a := h(1)$. Being in particular
a homomorphism of additive groups $(\Z,+) \to (R,+)$, $h$ satisfies, by Lemma 2 and
Lemma 1(v),
$$h(n) = h(n \cdot 1) = n\, h(1) = n a \qquad (n \in \Z). \tag{3.1}$$
Multiplicativity of $h$ applied to $1 = 1 \times 1$ gives
$$a = h(1) = h(1 \times 1) = h(1) \circ h(1) = a \circ a .$$
Hence, using Lemma 3 (subtraction identity) and $a \circ 1_R = a$,
$$a \circ (a - 1_R) = a \circ a - a \circ 1_R = a - a = 0_R .$$
By (NZD), $a = 0_R$ or $a - 1_R = 0_R$.

*If $a = 0_R$:* by (3.1) and Lemma 2 applied to the zero homomorphism (or directly:
$n\,0_R = 0_R$ for all $n$, by induction over $\Z$ using Lemma 1(i)), $h(n) = n\,0_R = 0_R$ for
all $n \in \Z$, i.e. $h$ is the zero homomorphism.

*If $a = 1_R$:* by (3.1), $h(n) = n 1_R = g(n)$ for all $n \in \Z$, i.e. $h = g$.

So the only ring homomorphisms $\Z \to R$ are the zero map and $g$, and $g$ is nonzero;
therefore $g$ is the unique nonzero ring homomorphism from $\Z$ into $R$. $\square$

**Remark.** Hypothesis (NZD) cannot be dropped: in the ring with unity $R = \Z \times \Z$ the
map $h(n) = (n,0)$ is a nonzero ring homomorphism different from $g(n) = (n,n)$.

## 4. Three standard facts

**Lemma 4.** Every subgroup $H$ of $(\Z,+)$ equals $n\Z = (n)$ for a unique integer $n \ge 0$.

*Proof.* *Existence.* If $H = \{0\}$, take $n = 0$. Otherwise $H$ contains some $h \neq 0$ and
also $-h$, hence contains a positive integer; by the well-ordering principle let $n$ be the
least positive element of $H$. As in step (c) of Theorem A, induction over $\Z$ gives $kn \in H$ for every
$k \in \Z$: indeed $0 \cdot n = 0 \in H$, and if $kn \in H$ then $(k \pm 1)n = kn \pm n \in H$
by closure of $H$ under $+$ and $-$. So $n\Z \subseteq H$. Conversely, let
$h \in H$ and write $h = qn + r$ with $q, r \in \Z$, $0 \le r < n$ (division algorithm). Then
$r = h - qn \in H$, and $0 < r < n$ would contradict the minimality of $n$; hence $r = 0$ and
$h = qn \in n\Z$. So $H = n\Z$.

*Uniqueness.* Suppose $m\Z = n\Z$ with $m,n \ge 0$. Then $n \in m\Z$ and $m \in n\Z$. If
$m = 0$ then $n \in \{0\}$, so $n = 0 = m$. If $m > 0$ and $n > 0$ then $m \mid n$ and
$n \mid m$ force $m = n$ (as both are positive). $\square$

Since $g$ is in particular a homomorphism of additive groups, $\ker g = \{n \in \Z : n 1_R = 0_R\}$
is a subgroup of $(\Z,+)$, so by Lemma 4 it equals $(n)$ for a unique $n \ge 0$. (It is in fact
an ideal of $\Z$; see Lemma 5.)

**Lemma 5 (First Isomorphism Theorem for rings).** Let $h : A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism
with kernel $K = \{a \in A : h(a) = 0_B\}$. Then $K$ is an ideal of $A$, $h[A]$ is a subring of
$B$, and
$$\bar h : A/K \to h[A], \qquad \bar h(a + K) := h(a)$$
is a well-defined ring isomorphism; in particular $A/K \cong h[A]$.

*Proof.* *$K$ is an ideal.* $K$ is a subgroup of $(A,+)$: $h(0_A) = 0_B$, and if $h(a) = h(b) = 0_B$
then $h(a - b) = h(a) - h(b) = 0_B$ (using that $h$ is an additive homomorphism). For $k \in K$
and $a \in A$, $h(a k) = h(a) \circ h(k) = h(a) \circ 0_B = 0_B$ and similarly
$h(k a) = 0_B \circ h(a) = 0_B$; so $ak, ka \in K$. Hence $K$ is a two-sided ideal and the
quotient ring $A/K$ exists, with operations $(a+K)+(a'+K) = (a+a')+K$ and
$(a+K)(a'+K) = a a' + K$. (These are well defined: if $a - a' \in K$ and $b - b' \in K$ then
$(a+b)-(a'+b') \in K$, and $ab - a'b' = a(b - b') + (a - a')b' \in K$ because $K$ is a two-sided
ideal.)

*$h[A]$ is a subring of $B$:* it is nonempty and closed under subtraction and multiplication,
since $h(a) - h(a') = h(a-a')$ and $h(a) \circ h(a') = h(a a')$.

*Well defined and injective.* For $a,a' \in A$,
$$a + K = a' + K \iff a - a' \in K \iff h(a-a') = 0_B \iff h(a) = h(a').$$
The implication "$\Rightarrow$" says $\bar h$ is well defined; "$\Leftarrow$" says it is injective.

*Surjective.* Immediate, since the codomain is $h[A]$.

*Homomorphism.* $\bar h\bigl((a+K)+(a'+K)\bigr) = \bar h\bigl((a+a')+K\bigr) = h(a+a') = h(a)+h(a') =
\bar h(a+K) + \bar h(a'+K)$, and likewise
$\bar h\bigl((a+K)(a'+K)\bigr) = h(a a') = h(a) \circ h(a') = \bar h(a+K) \circ \bar h(a'+K)$. $\square$

**Lemma 6.** If $p$ is prime, then $\Z_p = \Z/p\Z$ is a field.

*Proof.* $\Z_p$ is a commutative ring with unity $[1]_p$, and $[1]_p \neq [0]_p$ because
$p \ge 2$ does not divide $1$. Let $[a]_p \neq [0]_p$, i.e. $p \nmid a$. Since $p$ is prime, its
only positive divisors are $1$ and $p$, and $p \nmid a$, so $\gcd(a,p) = 1$. By Bézout's
identity there are $u,v \in \Z$ with $u a + v p = 1$, whence
$$[u]_p [a]_p = [ua]_p = [1 - vp]_p = [1]_p .$$
So every nonzero element of $\Z_p$ is invertible, and $\Z_p$ is a field. $\square$

## 5. Theorem C

**Theorem C.** Assume $R$ has no proper zero divisors. Then the kernel of $g$ is either
$(1)$ $(0)$, in which case $g$ is an isomorphism from $\Z$ onto $S$; or
$(2)$ $(p)$ for some prime $p$, in which case $S$ is isomorphic to the field $\Z_p$.

*Proof.* By Lemma 4 (applied to the subgroup $\ker g$ of $(\Z,+)$), $\ker g = (n)$ for a unique
integer $n \ge 0$. We show $n = 0$ or $n$ is prime.

First, $n \neq 1$: otherwise $\ker g = 1 \cdot \Z = \Z$, so $1 \in \ker g$, i.e.
$0_R = g(1) = 1_R$, contradicting $1_R \neq 0_R$.

**Case $n = 0$.** Then $\ker g = (0) = \{0\}$, and $g$ is injective: if $g(m) = g(m')$ then
$g(m - m') = g(m) - g(m') = 0_R$ (Theorem A(b)), so $m - m' \in \ker g = \{0\}$, i.e. $m = m'$.
By Theorem A, $g : \Z \to S$ is a surjective ring homomorphism; being also injective, it is a
bijective homomorphism, i.e. an isomorphism from $\Z$ onto $S$. This is alternative $(1)$.

**Case $n \ge 2$.** We claim $n$ is prime. Suppose not. Since $n \ge 2$ is not prime, it is
composite: by definition, an integer $n \ge 2$ is prime iff its only positive divisors are
$1$ and $n$, so $n$ has a positive divisor $a \notin \{1, n\}$, and since every positive divisor
of $n$ is at most $n$ we get $1 < a < n$. Put $b := n/a \in \Z$. From
$n = ab$ and $a > 1$ we get $b < n$, and from $a < n$ we get $b > 1$; so $1 < a < n$ and
$1 < b < n$. Because $\ker g = n\Z$ and $0 < a < n$, we have $a \notin \ker g$, i.e.
$g(a) \neq 0_R$; likewise $g(b) \neq 0_R$. But by Theorem A(a),
$$g(a) \circ g(b) = g(ab) = g(n) = 0_R ,$$
so $g(a)$ is a nonzero element annihilating the nonzero element $g(b)$, i.e. a proper zero
divisor of $R$ — contradicting (NZD). Hence $n =: p$ is prime and $\ker g = (p)$.

Applying Lemma 5 to the ring homomorphism $g : \Z \to R$, whose image is $S$ by Theorem A, we
obtain
$$S = g[\Z] \cong \Z / \ker g = \Z / p\Z = \Z_p ,$$
and $\Z_p$ is a field by Lemma 6. This is alternative $(2)$.

Since $n \ge 0$ and $n \neq 1$, the two cases $n = 0$ and $n \ge 2$ are exhaustive and mutually
exclusive, so exactly one of the alternatives $(1)$, $(2)$ holds. $\square$

## 6. Theorem D: the general case

**Theorem D.** Let $R$ be an arbitrary ring with unity (so $1_R \neq 0_R$), with $g$ and $S$ as
above. Then $\ker g = (n)$ for a unique integer $n \ge 0$, and $n \neq 1$; moreover
$$S \cong \Z/n\Z = \Z_n \qquad (\text{with } \Z_0 := \Z).$$
This $n$ is the characteristic of $R$. Without hypothesis (NZD), $n$ need be neither $0$ nor
prime, and $S$ need not be a field.

*Proof.* Lemma 4 applied to the additive subgroup $\ker g \le (\Z,+)$ gives $\ker g = (n)$ for a
unique $n \ge 0$, and $n \ne 1$ exactly as in Theorem C (else $1_R = g(1) = 0_R$). Lemma 5
applied to $g$, whose image is $S$ by Theorem A, gives $S \cong \Z/n\Z$; for $n = 0$ this reads
$S \cong \Z/\{0\} \cong \Z$, consistent with $\Z_0 := \Z$.

For the final assertion take $R = \Z_4$, which is a ring with unity $[1]_4 \neq [0]_4$. Here
$g(m) = m [1]_4 = [m]_4$ (induction over $\Z$, or Lemma 2 applied to the quotient homomorphism
$\Z \to \Z_4$ together with Lemma 1(v)), so $g$ is onto $\Z_4$, whence $S = \Z_4$ and
$\ker g = \{m : 4 \mid m\} = 4\Z = (4)$. The integer $4$ is neither $0$ nor prime, and $\Z_4$ is
not a field: $[2]_4 \ne [0]_4$, yet $[2]_4[2]_4 = [0]_4$, so $[2]_4$ has no inverse (if
$[u]_4[2]_4 = [1]_4$ then $[0]_4 = [u]_4 [2]_4[2]_4 = [1]_4[2]_4 = [2]_4$, a contradiction).
In particular $\Z_4$ is not isomorphic to any $\Z_p$ with $p$ prime, and (consistently with
Theorem C) $\Z_4$ does have proper zero divisors. $\square$

## 7. Remark on the degenerate convention

If one adopts the convention under which the null ring $R = \{0_R\}$ counts as a ring with
unity (with $1_R = 0_R$), then $R$ vacuously satisfies (NZD) — it has no nonzero elements at
all — while $g$ is the zero map, $S = \{0_R\}$, and
$$\ker g = \Z = (1),$$
which is neither $(0)$ nor $(p)$ for a prime $p$; moreover $g$ is then *not* a nonzero
homomorphism, so Theorem B fails as well (the zero map is the only homomorphism $\Z \to R$).
This degenerate case is excluded by the standing convention $1_R \neq 0_R$, which is the one
used in the source of the statement. Apart from it, Theorems A–D above establish the assertion
in full.
